ABAKAN, a river rising in the Altai chain, and falling into the Yenisei, in the vicinity of Minusinsk, after a NNE course of 200 m .- On its r. bank, 210 m. SSW of Krasnoïarsk, is a small town of the same name. Pop. 650, chiefly sable-hunters.

ABAKANSK, a town and fort in Siberia, on the Yenisei, in N lat. 54°, 125 m. SSW of Krasnoïarsk. Pop. 1,300, chiefly agricultural. This settlement was founded by Peter the Great in 1707. Sheltered by high mountains, it is considered the warmest place in Siberia: even tobacco and some fruits are grown here. Coal is found in the neighbouring mountain of Isek. At the passage of the Yenisei, below the ford, is a steep rock bearing Mogul and Tartar inscriptions; and near it are several ancient tombs.

ABASIA (LITTLE), the north-eastern, and smallest division of that region of Circassia called by the Circassians Tapanta, and by the Tartars Altikesek, or 'The Six Parts,' near the sources of the Kuban, and in the vicinity of the Karachaï. The population of this district are supposed by Gärbar to be descended from the ancient Magyar stem. Disunited by the intrigues of their Kabardian neighbours, a part of them were forced to take refuge among the Bashilbaizi who dwelt near the sources of the Talentschug and Urun rivers, to the N of the source of the Kúban; others fled to the Russians, who gave them settlements near the sources of the small streams which descend into the Kúban and the Kúma. These last were soon joined by numbers of the Altikeseks, and the Russian frontier-lines experienced the benefit of their presence in a supply of cheap provisions and excellent cavalry horses, while the markets of Taganrog received from them large droves of cattle, besides leather, wool, butter, honey, and wax. The Russian government relaxing in its attentions to them, they were so illused by the Chernomorskoi Cossacks, that yielding to the suggestions of Turkey, they fled in 1804 across the Kúban, whence however they returned in the succeeding year. …
ABAU, a river of Russia in the gov. of Courland, the principal tributary of the Vindau, which it joins on the r. bank about 10 m. below Goldingen.

ABINTZY, ABINZI, or ABINSK TATARS, a people of Asiatic Russia, inhabiting the district of Kusnesk, in the gov. of Tomsk, about 600 m. ESE of Tobolsk. They call themselves Abahar, an appellation which seems to indicate a primitive people; for, in the Tatar language, aba—whence this name is derived— signifies 'father.' The A. formerly inhabited the banks of the Tom, near Kusnesk, and might be regarded as a branch of the Tomski Tatars; but, when the Téléoutes quitted the White Mountains to establish themselves in their present location, the Abintzys -who were the weaker party, but did not choose to be driven farther to the north—ascended the Tom to ABI the high mountains, on the N of the lake of Teletskoi, in which they now dwell. The A. are divided into several aimaks or tribes, but pay tribute for scarcely more than 100 bows. In appearance, character, manners, language, and dress, the Abintzys perfectly resemble the Téléoutes. Their occupations are the rearing of cattle, the chase, fishing, the smelting of iron, and agriculture.
ABRO, a small islet of Russia, off the coast of Livonia, 3 m. S of Arensburg.

AC-METCHET, or AK-MESHID, the modern metropolis of the Crimea, now called Sympheropol by the Russians. It is finely situated near the centre of the peninsula, in the valley of the Salghyr, 20 m. NE of Baktschiserai, and 40 from Sevastopol, in 44° 57' N lat.; 963 m. from Moscow, and 1,408 from St. Petersburg. Both Heber and Clarke describe it as a poor place, formerly extensive, but since it fell into the hands of the Russians greatly fallen off in appearance. Kohl says that it contains, "like all the Russian new cities, many handsome houses decorated with green paint and rows of columns," and "streets of such a breadth that one can scarcely see across them." Of late years many improvements have been made upon it; and Dr. Lyall describes the cathedral as the handsomest ecclesiastical edifice he had seen in Russia. Yet a later visitor, Hommaire de Hell, laments that of the "palaces, mosques, and fine gardens," which adorned it when the residence of the Kalga sultan, "few traces now remain;" that "the tortuous streets, high walls, and rose-thickets of the old city" should have given place to the cold monotony of a Russian town; and that instead of building the new town on the banks of the river, it has been set "at the top of a great plateau." The pop., a medley of Russians, Tatars, Germans, Moldavians, Jews, Armenians, and Turks, is about 8,600. …

ACHTUBA, an arm of the Volga, which branches off from its E side, 6 m. above Tzaritzin, flows in a nearly parallel course with it and seldom at a greater distance than 10 or 12 m., and falls into the Caspian, near Krasnojarsk. The greater part of its course, of nearly 300 m., is through the steppes of Astrakhan. Its banks are inhabited by wandering Tartars of the Nogay horde; and in its environs Prof. Tauscher found numerous vestiges of ancient Tartar towns.
ACHTYRKA, a town and district of Russia, in the Ukraine, 45 m. W by N of Kharkov, near the Vorskla. The environs are fertile, and there are some woollen manufactures here. Pop. 12,788.
ACU'SHAH, a petty state of Dághistán, under the nominal authority of the shamkhal of Tarkú. Its pop., a Lesghian tribe, has been estimated at 10,000.
ADMIRALTY PENINSULA, a projection on the W coast of Novaïa Zemlïa, in N lat. 75°, between Glasoff bay and Maschigin bay.

AGOMI, a river of Siberia, rising in a lake on the NW declivity of the Stannovoi mountains, and flowing, by a NW course, to the Utchur, a head-branch of the Aldan.

AHWENDEAR, an islet in the Red sea; in N lat. 26° 36′, E long. 36° 10′; 6½ m. WSW of Sherm Demerah.—Moresby. AI, a river of Russia, an important affluent of the Ufa, which rises, in several head-streams, to the W of Mount Jurma, in the Ural chain, in the prov. of Orenburg, and after a course first SW and then NW, falls into the Ufa, on the l. bank, 15 m. below Meteli. The upper part of its valley is narrow and marshy; below the bend where it turns to the W it is deep, narrow, and rocky.—Murchison. AI, or Ay, a v. of Bavaria, in the circle of the Upper Danube, N of Illertissen. Pop. 167.
AIBAR, a v. in the Crimea, 26 versts [17 m.] S of Dürmeen, on the direct route from Perekop to Acmetchet.—Pallas.

AKSEENSKAIA, a town of Russia, in the territory of the Don Cossacks, 90 m. SW by S from Sarepta, on a stream flowing S to the Don. AKSERAT, [i. e. 'White palace,'] a town of Asiatic Turkey, the capital of a sanjak of the same name, 16 hours N by E of Karabunar, 94 m. SSE of Angora; in N lat. 38° 20' [Hamilton]; situated in an open and well cultivated valley, through which the Beyáysú flows into the salt lake of Kóch-hisar. ALASEI, or Alaseia, a large river of Siberia, rising in N lat. 67°, on a range of wooded hills called the Alasei, which branches from the main chain of the Stanovoi ridge in about N lat. 61° 30', E long. 147°, and runs up, through the Jakuti country, till it sinks into the Tundra or moss level on the shores of the Arctic ocean, forming the dividing ridge between the waters of the Indigirka on the W, and the Alasei on the E. The A. river receives a number of tributaries, some of which flow from the mountains, and others from different large lakes. Its general course is N, but it winds much, and empties itself into the sea by five arms, of which the eastern, called Lagoshkin, has a rapid current, and forms at its entrance an island 2 versts in length. It is 150 fath. broad 2 versts above the island. The next arm, 3½ versts to the W of the former, is called the Alaseiskoj Protok. The other three arms, going westwards, are sometimes mere dry channels.

ALBUTY, a name given in Northern Siberia to flat valleys which, though dried up in summer, are occasionally filled with water in spring, when they form lakes of various sizes, which form one of the peculiar features of that country. The rich alluvial soil when thus cleared of water is speedily covered with a luxuriant growth of fine grass, and the Jakuti never fail to settle near these fresh pastures. Hence the frequent occurrence of the term albut or albuty in the topography of this district. - Wrangel.

ALDA'N, a river of Siberia, a confluent of the Lena. It rises on the northern declivity of the Yablonoi Khrebet, between 127° and 129° E long, and runs in a NNE course nearly 400 m. to Aldanskaja. ALD It then turns NW by N, and after flowing more than 100 m. in that direction, bends WSW, and pursues that direction to its junction with the Lena, on the r. bank, 60 m. below Yakutsk. Wrangel found it 11 verst in breadth, with a rapid current at 90 versts above its junction with the Lena. Aldanskaja Perewos, in the valley of the A., is 424 ft. above sea-level. [Erman.]—A mountain-range, deriving its name from this river, rises with a steep ascent, from its eastern banks. Mount Kapitan, in this range, has an alt. of 4,263 ft. above sea-level; and from this mountain the surface of the country as far E as Ketanda, about 100 m. from Okotsk, has an average elevation of 2,500 ft. [Erman.] Cochrane says that the whole distance from Okotsk to Yakutsk-with the exception of a portage across a chain of mountains which confine the Arko, a large stream uniting with the Okota-might be accomplished in canoes by means of the Udoma a tributary of the Aldan. When the ice breaks upwhich usually happens in the month of May-vast masses are borne down the course of the A. with tremendous velocity.

ALTAI, an extensive mountain-system in Central Asia, which extends from 43° to 52° N lat., and from 87° to 97° E long. of Greenwich. But the term has been used by some geographers in a far more extensive application than that now indicated; giving it more than 100 degrees of longitudinal extent, and inducing the idea that a continuous uninterrupted range of lofty mountains forms the southern boundary of Western as well as Eastern Siberia, than which nothing can be more remote from truth. Erman too has shown that a totally different geological formation commences at the S extremity of the Baikal lake, and characterises the mountain-ranges of Kingan to Jablonoi Krebet, in which Pallas and others trace the prolongation of the Altai to the shores of the sea of Okotsk. Humboldt also denies the existence of any mountain-chain connecting the Altai ALT and the Ural on the other side of the continent, as the Krasnoyarsk chain is by some represented to do. In fact, the name Altai should be restricted to the great range which, running from SW to NE, separates Zungaria from Mongolia; and which, in ancient times, formed a great political as well as physical boundary in the northern part of the great central plateau of the Asiatic continent. The most prominent masses of the system thus defined are found between the parallels of 49° and 51° N. …

ALUPKA, a village of Russia, on the south coast of the Crimea, midway between Kutkucoy and Yursova, on a stream called the Stauris Usehen. It is picturesquely situated amidst groves of fruit-trees, and gardens, in which the olive and the pomegranate attain remarkable luxuriance. [Webster.] The scenery in this district of the coast of the Crimea is so remarkably beautiful that Clarke affirms it "will admit of no comparison with any other maritime district. Such fertility and rural beauty," he adds, "are perhaps nowhere else situate equally near to the waters of any sea, nor so surrounded by grand objects. The descent towards the shore is so steep and rapid that it seems as if the villages, with their groves and gardens, might be swept by heavy rains into the deep: at the same time cliffs hanging over them menace fearful ruin by the fall of rocks which every now and then break loose." [Travels, vol. ii., 4th 8vo. edn., p. 250.] Upon and amongst prodigious fragments of these fallen rocks, the v. and its gardens are situated.

ALUSHTA, a town of Russia, on the coast of the Crimea, between the mouths of the Temirdshi and the Mesarlik, on an isolated height, 20 m. E of Acmetchet. It formerly had a considerable population, and was the seat of an episcopate. It is built on a series of terraces, "so that the flat roof of one house serves as a promenade to the people of the upper one." [Webster.] The Chatyrdag is in the vicinity of this town. "We began its ascent," says Webster, "an hour after leaving A., and continued ascending an hour and a half, yet were still <math>\frac{3}{4}</math> of an hour from the top, although the height is only 1,200 ft."

ANADO'LI, ANATO'LIA, or NATO'LIA, the largest and most westerly of the pashaliks of Asia Minor, comprising upwards of one-half of the entire extent of the peninsular portion of Asiatic Turkey, or Asia Minor. It is bounded on the N by the Black sea; on the NE by the pash. of Sivas, from which, to a considerable extent, it is separated by the Kizil Irmak; on the SE by the pashaliks of Caramania and Ichil; on the S and W by the Mediterranean; and on the NW by the Hellespont, the sea of Marmora, and the straits of Constantinople. It stretches from N lat. 36° to 42°, and from E long. 26° to 34° 40'; and probably contains, exclusive of the numerous islands which skirt its western coasts, a superficies of 100,000 sq. m. …

MINGRELIA, a province of Asiatic Russia, bounded on the N by the Circassian districts; on the E by Imeritia Proper; on the S by Guriel; on the SW by the Black sea; and on the NW by the territory of the Abasses. The Risni is its principal river. It has an area of 2,365 sq. m., with a pop. estimated at from 60,000 to 100,000. They are in general inferior in personal appearance and physical strength to the mountaineers of the Caucasus, but obedient and faithful to their feudal chiefs. It is a mountainous region, intersected by deep valleys, "still as damp, hot, and subject to fevers as when Hippocrates described it under the name of Colchis." The most fertile tracts lie waste, only poisoning the atmosphere with the effluvia of their decomposed herbage. Vegetation is rapid, and fruits are produced without the care of grafting; but their flavour is not always the finest. The wine is good; and tobacco, rice, millet, and gomi are grown. The Mingrelians do not now cultivate flax, which in the time of Herodotus and of Strabo furnished the Colchians with the means of an important manufacture. The only object to which they appear to give any attention is the management of bees, and, in the district of Ledzgami, the rearing of the silk-worm. The honey of some cantons, where the Azalea pontica abounds, is bitter. …

ANAPA, a town of Circassia, in the country of the Abkhasses, on Sunjik bay, in the Black sea, 70 m. ESE of Theodosia, 46 m. from Kertche. This town, formerly 2 m. in circuit, is now a small hamlet, standing in a large plain in which the branches of the Caucasus terminate, and which stretches N and E towards the Kuban. It has a well-built khan, and is defended by a fortress, erected upon a rock about 100 ft. high, on the S side of the town. Towards the N the coast is low and marshy. Its pop. in 1824 was estimated by Marigny at 2,000. It exports hides, hare and sheep skins, tallow, wax, and honey; and the custom-house duties under the Porte amounted to from 15,000 to 40,000 piastres. Its roadsted is a little bay to the NE of the village. The anchorage is shallow and insecure. The site of A. originally belonged to a small Circassian tribe. In 1784, the Turks built A. to protect the Tartars who had taken refuge on the L bank of the Kuban, and the Nogois; and from that time, the productions of Circassia circulated chiefly through this new channel, as they had formerly done through Taman and Temruk, before these places were seized by Russia. ARCHANGEL, or ARCHANGELSKOE [i. e., 'the Land of the Archangel'], a prov. of Russia, on the shores of the Arctic ocean; bounded by the gov. of Tobolsk on the NE and E; by that of Wologda on the S and SE; by Olonetz on the SW; and by Finland on the NW. Its northern continental shores are washed by the Arctic ocean and the White sea; and for a considerable distance from the coast present a desolate and sterile appearance, with few signs of vegetation. It embraces the whole northern part of Russia in Europe, and includes the island of Nova Zembla. Between the Arctic ocean and its frontier conterminous with Wologda, it stretches over 8° from N to S. Its E limit is in 66°, and its W in 30° E long. Its area is estimated by Möller at 15,215 German, or 342,337 sq. m.; and by M. Kæppen at 750,906 sq. versts, or 15,519 German sq. m. As the latter calculation was carefully made upon Schubert's special map, it is probably a pretty close approximation to the fact; but in both admeasurements the superficies of the islands is included, which probably amounts to one-fourth of the whole. The surface is in general a continuous flat, covered either with sandy and mossy wastes, or pine and alder forests. The principal rivers are the Dwina and its affluents; and the Petshora and Onega. There are many lakes, amongst which are the Imandra, the Taposero, the Angosero, and the Koutno. …

KAPA (SEA OF), or KARSKOE MORE', a name given by Russian geographers to that portion of the Arctic ocean which lies to the S of Nova Zembla, between the coasts of European and Asiatic Russia. It is bounded by the island of Nova Zembla on the NW, and by a peninsular projection of the Asiatic gov. of Tobolsk on the SE. It lies between the meridians of 58° and 77° E, and the parallels of 69° and 76° 30' N. On the SE it is prolonged by a deep indentation called Karaskaia bay; on the SW it communicates by two channels, the straits of Kara and of Waygatz, with the sea to the W of Nova Zembla. The river Kara, which gives its name to the bay and gulf, discharges itself a little to the W of the bay of the same name.

SIBERIA, a great physical division of the Russian empire, comprising the extreme northern portion of the Asiatic continent between the Altai range and the Arctic ocean. The whole northern part of the continent has received the general appellation of ASIATIC RUSSIA. Including the Caucasian districts, the Russian territories in Asia stretch from the straits of Kaffa on the W to Behring's straits on the E; and from Cape Sallian and the island of Kura on the S, to Cape Taimura or North-east Cape on the N. The vast region called Siberia,—a name almost identical in pronunciation with the Russian word Seweria, or 'Country of the north,' and which has been vaguely applied to all the newly-discovered territories in this quarter, lies between the parallels of 45° and 78°, and the meridians of 60° and 190° E long. Its extreme length is nearly 4,000 m.; its greatest breadth, 1,870 m.; and its area exceeds 4,700,000 sq. m.; but it is only a comparatively narrow strip of the S part of this vast region that is available for the purposes of civilized life. The northern boundary runs along the coast of the Icy ocean, from the mouth of the Kara, in the gulf of Kariskai, to East cape. On the NE Behring's straits separates this territory from America; on the E the two seas of Kamtchatka and Okhotsk define the coast-outline. …

TUNGUSES, a native race of Asiatic Russia, who wander over the whole SE portion of that vast territory. They are first found on the banks of the Yenisei, whence they extend eastward to the sea of Okhotsk. In the south, however, they are mixed with the Mongols and Buriats; and on the borders of the northern ocean, they give place to the Yakuts and Samoyedes. To the W of the Yenisei, a few are mixed with the Tartars and Ostiaks; but in general the prov. of Irkutsk-proper is that of which they may be considered the denizens. They are of a middle size, of a robust constitution, and endowed with great agility. Their countenance bears a considerable resemblance to that of the Mongols, though it is larger, and still more flattened. They have small eyes, a smiling physiognomy, and long black hair, which they allow to flow freely over their shoulders. They employ themselves solely in hunting and fishing. They have no permanent abodes, but range through the woods and along the rivers, seldom remaining more than six days at a time in one spot. Their tents are formed of a few spars, put together in a conical shape, and covered with skins or with willow bark, which after being exposed for some time to the vapour of boiling water becomes equally flexible. Their arms are bows and arrows, with which they will attack the fiercest animals. …

AVARES, a khanate of Russia, in the Caucasus, extending between the Koïsou and Aksai, and bounded on the S by the Upper Samur and the snowy ridge of the Caucasus. It is extremely mountainous; and, except in the valleys, incapable of cultivation. The Avares form the most powerful of the Lesghiz tribes. They number 30,000, and are governed by an independent khan or chief. They speak a dialect of the Lesghian, and profess Mahommedanism. An annual subsidy of 10,000 rubles was, and perhaps is still paid them by Russia, in consideration of their abstaining from depredations on the adjacent provinces.

AVATCHA, or AWATSKA, a bay of Russia, in Asia, on the SE coast of Kamtschatka, at the mouth of a river of the same name, and of the Paratounka or Ilmitsh, in N lat. 52° 52', E long. 158° 47', forming a noble harbour. Its coast-line is about 27 m. in extent; and it is entered by a channel about 4 m. in length, and 2 m. in breadth. It varies from 14 to 18 ft. in depth. The highest tides rarely exceed 5 ft. It is enclosed on the SW and W by wooded hills; and, although its temperature falls below that of some of the more northern districts of the peninsula, it is never entirely, and but rarely partially frozen. This bay forms the principal Russian port on the Pacific, and is the only harbour on the coast of Kamtschatka accessible to large vessels. It contains several minor bays. One of these, Petropaulski, on which a town of the same name, formerly called Avatcha, is situated, and which is separated from the bay by a narrow neck of land, is one of the finest harbours in the world. About 20 m. N by E of Petropaulski, is the active volcanic mountain of Avatcha, 11,500 feet in height.

IMIRITIA, a principality of Asiatic Russia, situated in the Western Caucasian regions, and bounded on the N by the principal chain of Caucasus; on the E by Georgia; on the S by Akhalzike; and on the W by Guriel and Mingrelia. It is watered by the Rioni, and numerous tributary streams, the course of most of which is interrupted by cataracts. The Tzchenesstzquali separates it from Mingrelia. The climate is extremely mild; snow seldom lies on the ground, and the rivers are never frozen over. Much of the surface consists of rocks and mountains, interspersed with fertile valleys and plains. Abundance of fruit of the finest flavour grows wild, and the trunk of the vine is here known to attain 15 inches in diam. Entire hills are overgrown with olive, myrtle, laurel, chestnut, and valuable timber trees; and the lower grounds present almond, fig, quince, pear, and plum trees, the latter sometimes bearing twice a-year. Copious harvests of grain, also of cotton, hemp, and flax, are obtained. The pop. of the principality is computed at 20,000 families, whose personal appearance is superior to that of their neighbours, but they are in general an indolent, distrustful, and proud race, though distinguished by the virtue of hospitality. As nearly the whole inhabitants dwell in solitary hamlets, the country contains scarcely any towns except Cotatis or Kutais, the capital, situated on the r. …
BAGENDAISK, a town in Siberia, in the hilly country which separates the basins of the Angara and the Lena, at an alt. of 524 ft. above sea-level.
BAGORODSK, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 30 m. E of Moscow, on the r. bank of the Kliazma.

SELENGA, a considerable river of Siberia, which rises beyond the frontier, in the country of the Khalha-Mongols, where it receives the smaller streams of the Kharatal, the Orkhon, the Khilop, and the Iga; on approaching the frontiers of the Russian gov. of Irkutsk, it begins to be navigable, and flows from SE to NW, and falls by three mouths into the great Baikal lake. The Russians have founded several towns on its r. bank, particularly Verschnei-Oudinsk, Selenghinsk, and Kiakhta. See article BAIKAL.

hier: gov. of Tomsk > district of Turukhansk
txt: BAIKHA, a river of Siberia, in the gov. of Tomsk. It takes its rise in the E of the district of Turukhansk, runs towards the W, and after a course of 150 m. falls into the Turukhan 45 m. W of the town of that name.—To the N of this river another named Vernaia-Baikha falls also into the Turukhau.
BAKBULAN, a river of Russia, in the Kirghiz steppes, rising in the Khaltai mountains, and flowing into Lake Shin.
BALAGANSK, a town of Siberia, 60 m. NW of Irkutsk, on the l. bank of the Angora. Pop. in 1833, 372.

BALASCHEV, or BALASCHEW, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Saratov, upon the Khoper, a tributary to the Don. Pop. 2,000. To the N of this town are extensive forests; to the S, interminable heaths or steppes.
BALATOF, a town of Asiatic Russia, on the river Khoper, 146 m. from Saratov.
BALDOHN, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Courland, 20 m. E of Mitau, near the river Duna. There are sulphurous springs here.

BALTA, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Podolia, 21 m. S of Obgopol, on the Kodima river, a tributary of the Bug. Pop. 1,200. - Also an islet of Scotland, lying to the E of the isle of Unst, in the Shetland group, in N lat. 60° 41'. Balta sound, between Balta and Unst, is a bay 2 m. in length, and about half-a-mile broad, so completely shut in by the island of B. that, seen from a distance, it resembles a lake. Both sides of this bay are in a state of high cultivation. The islet is wholly composed of diallage rock, and its cliffs are peculiarly rugged. It formed the N point of the arc of the meridian measured by Roy

BAR, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Podolia, 40 m. N of Mohilev, on the river Row. Pop. 3,000. It is fortified; and is celebrated for the confederation of the Polish nobles, Pulaski, Potocki, and Krasinski, against the Russian government, which was entered into here on the 29th of Feb. 1768.—Also a district and town of Hindostan, in the prov. of Bahar, on the r. bank of the Ganges, 20 m. NE of Bahar. Area of district 166 sq. m. Pop. 96,950.—Also a commune of France, in the dep. and the cant. of Corréze, 6 m. N of Tulle. Pop. 1,228.—Also a river of France, in the dep. of Ardennes, rising near Butancy, and joining the Meuse on the l. bank, near Donchery, after a course of 45 m.

BARABA, a steppe or extensive plain on the western verge of Siberia, situated between the rivers Irtish and Obi. This steppe, exceeding 600 versts in length from N to S, and 400 in breadth from E to W, is a continued flat, diversified only by forests of birch-wood, and by lakes both salt and fresh. The soil and the climate are extremely favourable to agriculture: some of the lands are indeed low and marshy, but in general they are either covered with fine herbage, or with luxuriant crops of grain. The southern part of the plain, towards the Irtish and the mountains of Altai, is the driest, but it is likewise the most barren and the least adorned with wood. Deep forests spread over the N, and overshadow the lower banks of the Obi. The native pop. of this steppe are called by the Russians Barabinzes, or Barabinzians; and, from the diversity of their features, appear to be descended from several different tribes. They had been successively conquered by the Kirghises and Sungarians; and when Siberia was subdued by the Russians, could relate no particulars whatever of their history. The greater part of them appear from their physiognomy to be of Tartar origin; the long, half-opened eyes of others of them, indicate their descent from the Mongols; while the Kalmuk countenances of a third part of them bespeak their affinity with the Sungarians, their former conquerors. …

IRTISH, a river of Asia, which has its source in Sungaria, towards the SE extremity of the Great Altaï mountains, in N lat. 46° 45'. It runs first WNW through a wide valley enclosed on the ENE by the Great Altaï, and on the S by the Altaï-Alintopa; issues thence on the W through Lake Taisan, or Kong-ko-lu, in the Chinese territory, and flowing N to the confluence of the Narim, enters Asiatic Russia; traverses, with great velocity, in a WNW direction, the steppes in the E part of the prov. of Omsk; thence bends its course, first N, then WNW, into the gov. of Tobolsk, till it reaches the town of that name, when it again curves N, and, after considerable sinuosities, reaches the Obi, which it joins, having run after a longer course than the Obi itself, on the l. bank, a little above Samarovo, and 150 m. W of Surgut, in N lat. 60° 45'. It has a total course of about 1,950 m., of which 720 m. are within the Chinese empire, 750 m. in the prov. of Omsk, and 480 m. in the gov. of Tobolsk. At its point of junction with the Obi, it has a width of 13 verst, and a depth of 50 ft.; while the Obi has a width of 10 versts, and is 300 ft. deep. Its principal affluents are in the Chinese empire, on the r., the Boroi, Kaba, Kurtchum, and Narim; in the prov. of Omsk, the Bukhtarma, Ulba, Uba, and Om, on the r., and the Tchar-Gurban, Tchaganka, Tunduk, and Kamishlovka, on the I.; and in the gov. …
BARANOVKA, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Volhynia, near the l. bank of the Slutch, 60 W of Jitomir.

BARANTCHINSK, a mining village of Russia, in the gov. of Perm, in the district and 69 m. SSW of Verkhofourie, on the Targil, and near the E base of the Ural mountains. It has blast and fining furnaces. The village and works belong to the Crown, and are under the joint administration of the mining government of Bogoslovsk and Blagodat.

txt: BARGOUZIN, or BARGUZIN, a town of Siberia, cap. of the district of the same name, in the gov. and 250 m. NE of Irkutsk, on the river Bargouzin, which, after a course in a SSW direction of 240 m. falls into Lake Baikal, in N lat. 53° 15'. The town possesses a wooden fort. In the environs are thermal springs and salt lakes.

BARISH, a river of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Simbirsk, which takes its rise in the S of the dist. of Syzran, passes Karsoun, and, after a course in a general direction from SE to NW of 120 m., falls into the Soura. This river formerly constituted the boundary between the territory of the Nogais Tatars and Russia.
BARRENOI (CAPE), a mass of rocks projecting into the sea, on the coast of Siberia, between Cape Shelotskoi and the mouth of the Kovyma.

BASHKIRS, or BASHKURS, a numerous tribe in the Russian gov. of Orenburg. They speak the Tartar dialect, and appear to be of Turco-Mongolian origin. They are Mahommedan Sunnites in religion, and in their general habits and manners differ little from other Tartar tribes. Their principal wealth consists in their flocks, cattle, horses, and camels; they are also celebrated for their management of bees; and they cultivate rye, barley, wheat, oats, and millet. Their horses are a strong and beautiful breed. The Bashkirs form excellent horsemen, and supply the Russian army with about 3,000 cavalry, who are armed with a bow and lance, in addition to a carabine and pistol; and protected by a helmet and coat-of-mail. They are divided into 12 cantons, which are subdivided into clans and villages. Their number does not probably fall short of 500,000; as there are above 72,000 men of from 17 to 45 years of age on the military muster roll, who pay no taxes, but hold themselves in readiness for foreign service, besides defending the frontier towards the Kirghiz steppe.—Rechberg.—Pallas.—Dahl.
BASHLI, a town of Circassia, in Daghistan, in N lat. 42° 25′, 24 m. NW of Derbent.
BATKALUISH, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Astrakhan, 80 m. SW of Astrakhan, in N lat. 45° 35'.
BATURIM, a town of Russia, in the Ukraine, on the Sem river, 80 m. ESE of Czernigov.

txt: BAOUSK, or Bausk, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Courland and dist. of Mitau, at the confluence of the Memel and Alass, 40 m. above the entrance of the Aa into the gulf of Livonia, and 20 m. SE of Mitau. It is ill-built, but possesses considerable commerce in grain, and has extensive breweries. Pop. 936.
BAUSKE, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Courland, near the source of the Aa. Pop. 1,200.
BAZALETHI, a district of Asiatic Russia, in the prov. of Georgia, on the r. bank of the Aragui. It is fertile in grain, barley, and millet.
BAZALIA, a village of Russia, in the gov. of Volhynia, in the district and 30 m. W of Staro- Konstantinof. Pop. 350.

LENA, a noble river of Eastern Siberia, which has its source in the gov. of Irkutsk, on the NW side of the lofty granitic mountains of Baïkal, 30 m. from the W bank of the lake of that name, in N lat. 53° 20', E long. 106° 10'. It runs first N, then NE; becomes navigable at Katchuk or Kotshuga, only 50 m. from its source; enters into the prov. of Yakutsk, near Krestovskoï; on reaching Yakutsk, where it is a wide and noble river, it takes a nearly N direction, and proceeds to the Arctic ocean, which it enters 700 m. below Yakutsk, by numerous mouths, in N lat. 73°. Its principal affluents are the Kirenga, Vitima, Olekma, Talbatchim, Aldan, on the r., and on the l. the Kuta, Viliui, and Mouna. The basin of the L., which is of considerably smaller extent than that of the Yenisei and Obi, is enclosed on the S by the mountains of Baikal and of Stanovoi, on the SE by the latter, on the E by a range of low hills by which it is separated from the basins of the Indighirka and Yana, and on the W by another low ridge running in the direction of the basins of the Yenisei and Olenek. The length of this river is upwards of 2,000 m. Its course is sinuous, and its current, as its name denotes, sluggish. …

BECHTAV, an insulated mountain in the Russian gov. of Orenburg, rising rapidly 3,000 ft. above the plain, and 4,000 ft. above the level of the Black sea. Its five conical summits have given it its name, which, in the Nogay language, signifies 'the Five mountains.' The rock of which it consists is a white trachyte, with small crystals of glassy feldspar. Its base is covered by strata of calcareous rock; and several hot ferruginous springs issue from this rock. There are also hot sulphureous springs at some versts distance.—Kupffer.

BEIDARY, or BAIDARY, a valley of Russia, in the S of the Crimea. It is watered by the Targouna, and bathed on the S by the Black sea; and from its beauty and fertility, strikingly contrasting with the wildness of the adjacent mountain district, has been called the Tempe of the Taurida. It contains 5 villages.

BEIKERMAN, a town of Russia, in the Crimea, and dist. of Simferopol, in the vicinity of which is a quarry of excellent soap-stone, large quantities of which are exported to Constantinople by way of Balaklava.

BEJETSK, a town of Russia, in the gov. and 60 m. NNE of Twer, near the Mologa. Pop. 4,000. An annual fair is held here, at which considerable quantities of grain, iron, silk and cotton stuffs, are disposed of.—The pop. of the district of B. in 1836 was 139,439.

BEJETSK, a town of Russia, in the gov. and 60 m. NNE of Twer, near the Mologa. Pop. 4,000. An annual fair is held here, at which considerable quantities of grain, iron, silk and cotton stuffs, are disposed of.—The pop. of the district of B. in 1836 was 139,439.
BEKHOF, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Courland, W of Mitau.

txt: BELAIA-TSERKOV, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Kiev, and the district of Vasilkov, on the l. bank of the Ros, 16 m. NW of Taratsha. It is remarkable for a victory gained here by the Poles over the Prekop Tartars in 1626.

txt: BELBEK, a river of Russia, in the peninsula of and receiving numerous springs and tributaries from the mountain-valleys of Ousenbakh. In its upper course, it is called Kabarta; at Albat it first receives the name of Belbek .- Pallas.

hier: district of Belebei > government of Orenburg
txt: BELEBEI, a town of Russia, cap. of the dist. of the same name, in the gov. and 165 m. NW of Orenburg, and 85 SW of Oufa, on the Belebeika. It is much resorted to by invalids. Pop., consisting chiefly of Cossacks, 700. The district of B. is intersected by a chain of lofty mountains. The principal rivers BEL by which it is watered are the Dioma, Ik or Belebeika, and Ouz.

BELEBEI, a town of Russia, cap. of the dist. of the same name, in the gov. and 165 m. NW of Orenburg, and 85 SW of Oufa, on the Belebeika. It is much resorted to by invalids. Pop., consisting chiefly of Cossacks, 700. The district of B. is intersected by a chain of lofty mountains. The principal rivers BEL by which it is watered are the Dioma, Ik or Belebeika, and Ouz.
BELIKI, a town of Russia, in the gov. and 25 m. SSW of Poltava, in the district and 10 m. NNE of Kobyliaki, on the r. bank of the Vorskla.
BELILOVKA, or BIELOVKA, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Kiev, in the district and 17 m. ESE of Makhnova, on a tributary of the Ros.

BELKI, or BIELKI, a name generally given by the Russians in Siberia to any range of mountains covered with perpetual snow, but especially to those which detach themselves from the ramifications of the Little Altai, between the Katunaia and the Irtish, and between 50° and 52° N lat., and 82° 20' and 85° 20' E long. These mountains differ considerably in their structure and aspect from all the other mountain-ranges in this region; and nowhere present insulated needles and steep peaks. The Belki are in fact branches of the Snowy mountains called Kholzun, which run towards the W and N. These branches are six in number: the Belki of the Ulba, of the Uba, of the Tighirik, of the Korgon, of the Anui, and of the Bashalak.—The Belki of the Ulba appear between the Turgusson and the Ulba or Gromolowka, in 50° 20' N lat. Their rocks are chiefly composed of serpentine, of jasper, breccia, and porphyry.—To the NW of these are the Belki of the Uba, between the Great and the Little Uba. The geological structure of this range is the same as that of the preceding. It is rich in copper. The mines of Kriukovskoi are the most celebrated. -The Belki of Tighirik extend between the Great Uba and the Inia. To the W they reach to the river from which they derive their name and to the Bielaia; on the E they are separated from the Belki of Korgon by the Kair Kumin, an affluent of the Tsharysh. …

BELOGOLOVSKA, a town of Kamtschatka, at the entrance of the river of the same name into the sea of Okotsk.

BELNA, or Belnum, Beaune in the French dep. of Cote-d'Or. BELNA, BEAUNE in the French dep. of Loiret. BELOGRADUM, BIELGOROD in the Russian gov. of Kursk. BELSIA, BEAUCE in the French dep. of Eure-et- Loir.

JALPUKH, a river of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Bessarabia, which has its source in the district and 45 m. SW of Bender; runs S, and throws itself into a lake of the same name, in the district and 30 m. NNW of Ismail, and after a course of about 90 m. Its principal affluents are the Salutza on the r., and on the l. the Lunga.—The lake of J. is 39 m. in length, and about 6 m. in breadth, and opens by several wide outlets on the S into the Danube. It abounds with fish.

txt: BENIAKONI, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Grodno, in the district and 20 m. N of Lida.
BERCHAD, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Podolsk, in the district and 15 m. NNE of Olgopol, and 28 m. SE of Bratslav, on the Beradka. Pop. 1,500.

hier: gov. of Ekaterinoslav > gov. of Taurida
txt: BERDA, a river of Russia in Europe, which takes its rise near the fort of Aleksievkaia, runs along the frontiers of the gov. of Ekaterinoslav and Taurida, and after a course, in a general direction from N to S, of 63 m., falls into the sea of Azov 6 m. S of Petrovskaia.

hier: gov. of Volhynia > district of Jitomir
txt: BERDITCHEF, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Volhynia, in the district and 20 m. S of Jitomir. It is ill-built, but possesses several churches, and a Carmelite convent containing a celebrated image of the Virgin, on which a crown of gold was conferred by Pope Benedict in 1753. B. has long been celebrated for its fairs, four of which are held annually, and the trade of which consists in grain, wine, honey, wax, leather, and horses and cattle, amounting in yearly value to the sum of £800,000. At the principal horse-fair, there is sometimes a show of 40,000 horses; and the seigneurs of the country attend it with their families, and remain encamped in the neighbourhood of the town for three weeks. The pop., consisting chiefly of Jews, is estimated at 20,000.

BERDIANSK, a town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Taurida, at the mouth of the Berda, on the sea of Azov, 250 m. NE of Simferopol. Its port is one of the best on the sea of Azov, and Mariapol is being deserted for it. Pop. in 1840, 1,258. Its chief export is wheat.—Also a cape on the coast of the sea of Azov, 211 m. WSW of Bielosarai.
BERESHKI, a town of Russia, in the gov. of Volhynia, on the Slutsh, NE of Bereshniza.
BERESHNIZA, a town of Russia, in Volhynia, on the Görun, NE of Luzk.

hier: gov. of Minsk > district of Borrizoff
txt: BERESINO, or Beresna, a small town of Russia, in the gov. of Minsk, in the district of Borrizoff, on the l. bank of the Beresina, 44 m. NE of Minsk.
